subtype: Pained and tearful in adult life [Mismatch]
passage: In the office pantry after the quarterly review, Mohit found Sudha standing with her back to the room, wiping her eyes with her dupatta. He stopped in the doorway. He couldn't tell whether it was the review, something at home, or a message from her family. He said quietly, "Do you want company, or should I leave you be?" Sudha gave a wet laugh. "Stay if you like. It's good news, actually. I got the promotion, and my father would have loved to hear it." She kept crying, and Mohit filled a glass of water and set it beside her without saying anything. After a while she said, "Thanks for not guessing." He said, "I nearly did."

qa.q: What did Mohit ask Sudha in the pantry?
qa.a: He asked whether she wanted company or should he leave her be.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling as she cried?
qa.a: Mixed feelings, glad about the promotion and sad that her father cannot hear it; the tears alone could not have told Mohit which.

qa.q: What did Mohit do that respected Sudha?
qa.a: He asked instead of guessing, offered the choice of company or privacy, and brought water.

qa.q: How might Mohit have felt before he asked?
qa.a: Uncertain, since he did not know whether the tears were about the review or about home.

grounding: A young adult cries from mixed feelings at work, and a colleague asks and offers privacy instead of guessing the cause from the tears.

subtype: Pained and tearful in adult life [Mismatch]
passage:
Subject: About this morning

Dear Preeti,
I wanted to write because I left the meeting so quickly. I got tearful when the client shouted about the delay, and I didn't want to fall apart in front of everyone. It wasn't only the shouting. I've slept badly for a week and my grandmother is unwell, so it all came out at once. I'm okay now, just tired. Thank you for pausing the call and asking if I wanted water. I appreciated that you didn't ask me to explain there. If it's alright, I'd like fifteen minutes with you tomorrow to go through what the client actually needs.

Jagdish

qa.q: What did Preeti offer during the call?
qa.a: Preeti paused the call and asked if Jagdish wanted water.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling in the meeting, and what else was behind it?
qa.a: Jagdish felt tearful and did not want to fall apart in front of everyone; the shouting was only part of it, alongside a week of poor sleep and a grandmother being unwell.

qa.q: What could Preeti reply to Jagdish?
qa.a: Preeti can say it is good to hear Jagdish is okay, agree to the fifteen minutes and offer support if Jagdish needs time.

qa.q: How might Preeti have felt seeing Jagdish tearful?
qa.a: Concerned, and perhaps unsure how to help; pausing the call and offering water shows care without pushing.

grounding: A young adult who was tearful at work explains that the cause was mixed, since tears alone do not show it, and appreciates a colleague who gave privacy.

subtype: Contemptuous and disgusted in relationships and work [Regulating]
passage: I'm Farida, and I noticed it first in my head: whenever Nandini spoke in meetings I heard a sneer. "Here she goes again." I rolled my eyes inwardly, and once, a little, outwardly. I didn't like who that made me. So I named it to myself, contempt, and took a break before the next meeting by walking around the block. Then I asked Nandini for coffee and said, "When you send the long updates, I find myself getting impatient. Can we agree on a short summary first?" She looked startled, then said, "I didn't realise. Sure, a summary first works." The sneer didn't vanish, but it lost some of its grip. I've stopped rehearsing her flaws in my head.

qa.q: Where did Farida walk before the next meeting?
qa.a: Around the block.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling on hearing the sneer inside?
qa.a: Contempt and impatience towards Nandini, and discomfort at feeling it.

qa.q: What made Farida's coffee conversation constructive?
qa.a: Farida described Farida's own reaction to the behaviour without insults and proposed a concrete fix.

qa.q: How might Nandini have felt when Farida raised the topic?
qa.a: Startled at first, but her "I didn't realise" suggests she was open to it.

grounding: A young adult notices contempt in their own thoughts about a colleague, names it, takes a break and raises the concern respectfully.

subtype: Contemptuous and disgusted in relationships and work [Regulating]
passage: Note from Preeti, senior manager. Vijay asked for ten minutes after the sprint review. He said he had been catching himself rolling his eyes at a teammate's sloppy commits, and that a thought like "he doesn't even care" kept repeating. He said he didn't like the feeling and wanted to handle it before it showed in meetings. I asked what he had tried. He had taken a walk each afternoon and written down what specifically bothered him: missing tests, no notes. Then he had asked the teammate to pair on the next task and add a short checklist. I told Vijay to keep raising the concern respectfully and privately, and to tell me if it does not ease, because contempt can wear a team down. I have asked for a review of the checklist in two weeks.

qa.q: What had Vijay written down about what bothered him?
qa.a: Missing tests and no notes.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling about the teammate?
qa.a: Irritation and contempt, with a thought like "he doesn't even care," which he disliked in himself.

qa.q: What could Vijay do if the feeling does not ease?
qa.a: He can tell Preeti, keep the private respectful check-ins with the teammate, and keep taking breaks.

qa.q: How might the teammate feel about being asked to pair and use a checklist?
qa.a: Possibly surprised or defensive, though a pairing invitation is a respectful way to raise it and may be welcome.

grounding: A young professional notices contempt for a teammate, names it, takes a break and raises the concern respectfully, seen and guided by a manager.

subtype: Hostile and furious de-escalation [Regulating]
passage: I'm Rajni, and I work at a ration-card help desk. One afternoon Vishal came in furious because his form had been rejected for the second time. He slammed his hand on the counter and shouted that we were useless. My heart raced and my first urge was to shout back. Instead I lowered my voice, took a half step back and said, "I can see this has been really frustrating. Let me look at the reason together with you." He was still loud, but he stopped hitting the counter. I said I couldn't change the rule, but I could tell him exactly what was missing so he could fix it that day. I also kept my hand near the bell for the security guard. If he hadn't calmed down, I would have walked away and called the guard.

qa.q: Why was Vishal furious?
qa.a: His form had been rejected for the second time.

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling as Vishal shouted, and how was it handled?
qa.a: Rajni's heart raced and the urge was to shout back, but Rajni spoke more quietly and stepped back.

qa.q: Why did Rajni keep a hand near the bell?
qa.a: Safety comes first, so Rajni was ready to get the guard if calm did not work.

qa.q: How might Vishal have felt when Rajni offered to look at the reason with him?
qa.a: Possibly heard, and a little less angry, since he stopped hitting the counter, though he was still loud.

grounding: A young adult facing a furious person speaks more quietly, keeps distance, offers a calm way out and keeps safety in mind.

subtype: Hostile and furious de-escalation [Regulating]
passage: Note from Irawati, clinic supervisor. At 4 pm a visitor stood at the desk and shouted at Asif about the wait, moving closer and jabbing a finger. Asif kept his hands visible and his voice low. He said, "You've waited a long time and I'm sorry it's been so hard. I can't change the queue, but I can check where your name is and tell you how long it's likely to be." The visitor kept shouting for a while. Asif stepped back and offered a chair away from the counter and a glass of water. When the shouting turned to threats, he said calmly, "I want to help, but I can't do it while I'm being threatened," and signalled me. I came over, and the visitor left after a minute. I thanked Asif and suggested a break; his hands were shaking.

qa.q: What did Asif offer the visitor besides a chair?
qa.a: A glass of water.

qa.q: What might Asif have been feeling while his hands shook?
qa.a: Probably shaken or scared after the threats, though he stayed calm outwardly.

qa.q: Why was signalling Irawati the right move?
qa.a: When calm did not work and threats began, safety meant getting help.

qa.q: How might the visitor have felt in the waiting area?
qa.a: Frustrated and helpless about the wait, which may explain the shouting though it does not excuse threats.

grounding: A young adult facing a furious visitor lowers his voice, keeps distance, offers a calm way out and gets help when threats begin, seen by a supervisor.

subtype: Apologetic and guilty in adult responsibility [Regulating]
passage: Twenty minutes before the client call, Ishita saw she had sent Pranav's draft budget instead of the final one. Her chest went cold. The call couldn't be moved. She didn't hide it or spiral. She typed to Pranav, "I sent the wrong file to the client at 2:10. It was mine to check and I didn't. I've asked them to ignore it and I'm sending the right one now. I'll add a check step so it doesn't repeat." Pranav read it standing in the lift, a bit stunned. He wrote, "Thanks for telling me straight away. Call them, I'll join." Ishita felt a wave of guilt but didn't add more apologies. After the call she said one clear sorry to Pranav and got on with the next task.

qa.q: What did Ishita send by mistake?
qa.a: Pranav's draft budget instead of the final one.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling when she saw the mistake?
qa.a: Her chest went cold and later she felt a wave of guilt, but she acted instead of spiralling.

qa.q: What made Ishita's apology fit the harm?
qa.a: She named the specific error, fixed it and added a check step, without over-apologising.

qa.q: How might Pranav have felt reading her message?
qa.a: Stunned at first, but grateful for the clear and quick telling, as his reply shows.

grounding: A young professional names a work error at once, apologises specifically and repairs it under time pressure, without over-apologising.

subtype: Apologetic and guilty in adult responsibility [Regulating]
passage: Zainab realised in the metro that she had left the gas on low under the dal that morning, and that Aditi, her flatmate, must have come home to a smoky flat and a burnt pot. Aditi had texted only, "Please call." Zainab's stomach knotted. That evening, standing in the kitchen doorway, she said, "I left the gas on and forgot the dal. I'm sorry for the smell, and for the risk. I've bought a timer for the kitchen and I'll cook the next three dinners." Aditi, arms crossed, said, "It was scary." Zainab nodded. "I know." She didn't launch into a list of how awful she was. She scrubbed the pot, and Aditi, after a while, dried it.

qa.q: What did Zainab buy for the kitchen?
qa.a: A timer.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling in the metro?
qa.a: Her stomach knotted, so she was anxious and guilty about the smoky flat.

qa.q: How could Zainab keep her apology in proportion?
qa.a: She can name what happened, say sorry for the effect and repair with a concrete change, without long self-blame.

qa.q: How might Aditi have felt coming home?
qa.a: Scared and annoyed at coming home to smoke, as Aditi's crossed arms and "It was scary" show. 😔

grounding: A young adult who made a mistake at home names it, apologises specifically and repairs, with amends that match the harm.

subtype: Shy, embarrassed and ashamed in adult settings [Regulating]
passage: In Gothenburg, Oskar mixed up two client names in front of the whole department, and someone laughed. His face flushed, and for the rest of the meeting he spoke only when asked. At lunch he took his sandwich to a quiet corner. Sofia, from the next desk, sat down anyway and said, "Last month I called the CEO by the wrong first name. In an email." Oskar blinked and gave a small smile. She added, "Tomorrow, would you like to go over the next slide together before the call?" He nodded slowly. The next day he said just one line in the meeting, about the deadline, and his voice shook only slightly. It was a small step. By Friday he had asked a question.

qa.q: What did Oskar mix up?
qa.a: Two client names.

qa.q: What was Oskar feeling for the rest of the meeting?
qa.a: Embarrassed and ashamed, since his face flushed and he spoke only when asked.

qa.q: What small step helped Oskar?
qa.a: Speaking one line the next day, after preparing with Sofia.

qa.q: How might Sofia's story about the wrong first name help Oskar?
qa.a: It shows that public mistakes happen to others too, so his feels more ordinary. 🙂

grounding: A young adult withdraws after a public mistake, and a supportive colleague treats it as ordinary and helps him take small steps.

subtype: Shy, embarrassed and ashamed in adult settings [Regulating]
passage: At the cricket club's Sunday nets, Pooja dropped an easy catch in the practice match while the whole club watched. Someone groaned. Her ears burned, and she turned away and spent the second half fielding at the boundary, far from everyone. In the changing room she said she might skip next week. Vasudha, the senior player, sat down and said, "Everyone drops the easy ones. I dropped one in a league match last year, in front of my parents." She didn't tell Pooja not to feel bad. She asked, "Want to do ten catches with me before nets next week? Just us." Pooja hesitated, then nodded. The next Sunday, after catching seven of ten, she asked to stand at slip.

qa.q: Where did Pooja field in the second half?
qa.a: At the boundary, far from everyone.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling after she dropped the catch?
qa.a: Embarrassed and ashamed, since her ears burned, she pulled away and she considered skipping next week.

qa.q: How did Vasudha help Pooja return?
qa.a: She shared her own dropped catch, offered private practice and a small step.

qa.q: How might the club see the dropped catch?
qa.a: As an ordinary slip, since Vasudha says everyone drops the easy ones; the groan was probably a passing reaction.

grounding: A young adult withdraws after a public mistake at a club, and a supportive senior treats it as ordinary and offers a small private step.

subtype: Thoughtful, interested and doubtful in meetings [Interpreting]
passage:
Subject: Quick check after today's meeting

Dear Rafiq,
While I was presenting the pricing plan today, I noticed you paused, wrote something down and raised your eyebrows at slide four. I found myself guessing: interested? doubtful? I realised I couldn't tell from a pause, and I didn't want to assume. Could you tell me what you were thinking? If you have doubts about slide four, I'd like to hear them, and if the eyebrow was about something else entirely, that's useful to know too. I'm free after 3 tomorrow, or you can reply here. 🙂

Thanks,
Jahnavi

qa.q: At which slide did Rafiq's eyebrows go up?
qa.a: Slide four.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi unsure and slightly worried about while watching Rafiq?
qa.a: Whether Rafiq was interested or doubtful; Jahnavi saw it could not be told from a pause.

qa.q: Why is Jahnavi's direct question better than guessing?
qa.a: Pauses and raised brows suggest interest or doubt but never prove it, while asking gets Rafiq's actual view.

qa.q: What might Rafiq have meant by the raised eyebrows?
qa.a: Possibly doubt, possibly interest, or something unrelated to slide four; Jahnavi leaves all of it open.

grounding: A young professional reads a colleague's pause, note-taking and raised brows as ambiguous signals and asks for that colleague's view.

subtype: Thoughtful, interested and doubtful in meetings [Interpreting]
passage: I'm Noor. In my early meetings I read every face like a code. Thomas, my senior, would go quiet and write in his notebook while I presented, and I decided he thought my idea was weak. I stumbled through the rest, sweating. Afterwards I heard him tell a colleague it was "the best idea today." I was floored. Later I realised the notebook was just how he thinks. Now, when a colleague is quiet, I ask, "Thomas, what's your take on this?" Half the time he has a concern I hadn't considered; half the time he's already sold. Either way, I no longer guess. A pause is just a pause until someone says what's in it.

qa.q: What did Thomas do in the meetings while Noor presented?
qa.a: He went quiet and wrote in his notebook.

qa.q: What was Noor worried about when Thomas wrote in his notebook?
qa.a: That Thomas thought Noor's idea was weak, so Noor stumbled through the rest.

qa.q: What does Noor do now when a colleague is quiet?
qa.a: Noor asks directly for their take.

qa.q: Why might Thomas have stayed quiet while Noor presented?
qa.a: The notebook was just how he thinks, so his silence was not a judgment, though Noor only found that out afterwards.

grounding: A young professional learns that a senior's silence and note-taking signal thought, not doubt, and asks for views instead of guessing.

subtype: Surprised, relieved and worried at work [Interpreting]
passage: Note from Vijay, department head. After the restructuring announcement, Sarita, a junior analyst, noticed her teammates. She saw one colleague's eyes widen and their voice go tight, and another let out a long sigh and drop their shoulders. Instead of concluding anything, she went to each in turn and said, "That was a lot to hear. How are you doing with it?" The first colleague said they were worried about their contract. The second said they were relieved that their project was safe. Sarita listened to each without promising anything. She told me later that she had guessed wrong about the second, taking the sigh for gloom. I have asked her to share what she learned about checking in with the team leads.

qa.q: What did Sarita say to each colleague?
qa.a: "That was a lot to hear. How are you doing with it?"

qa.q: What was the second colleague feeling?
qa.a: Relief that their project was safe, though Sarita had guessed gloom from the sigh.

qa.q: Why was Sarita's check-in wise?
qa.a: Cues suggest feelings but not their cause, so a calm question found the real reasons.

qa.q: How might the first colleague have felt when Sarita asked?
qa.a: Perhaps supported and listened to, even though nothing was promised.

grounding: A young professional reads a colleague's widened eyes and a sigh at news of restructuring as signals of feeling, not cause, and checks in calmly.

subtype: Surprised, relieved and worried at work [Interpreting]
passage: Thursday, 9 pm. Vidya's log. Today the manager announced that the client had approved our proposal. Raghav's eyes went wide, then he exhaled loudly and put his head in his hands for a second. My first thought was, he's disappointed? Then his voice came out tight: "Well. That's great." I nearly walked away. Instead, at the tea machine I said, "You looked hit by that news. Everything okay?" He laughed. "I'm so relieved I can't think. I've been afraid we'd lose the project since March." I'd have got it completely wrong. He is also a bit worried, he said, because now we have to deliver by June. Note to self: cues tell me something's up, not what. Asking took ten seconds, and he said thanks. 🙂

qa.q: What did Raghav say at the tea machine?
qa.a: He said he was so relieved he could not think, and that he had been afraid they would lose the project since March.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling when he put his head in his hands?
qa.a: Relief mixed with worry about delivering by June, though Vidya first guessed disappointment.

qa.q: What would you advise Vidya to do on seeing a colleague's odd reaction next time?
qa.a: Vidya can ask a calm, short question, as in the log.

qa.q: How might Raghav have felt when Vidya checked in?
qa.a: Glad to be asked, since he thanked Vidya and shared both the relief and the worry.

grounding: A young professional reads a colleague's widened eyes, loud exhale and tight voice at news of approval, guesses wrong, and learns to check in.

subtype: Deadpan and impassive as professional style [Mismatch]
passage: In the hospital records office, Aadhya's face never changed. When the auditor found an error, her expression stayed flat; when the team celebrated a clean audit, she nodded once. New colleague Ira read it as coldness and felt shut out. For weeks she guessed: was Aadhya bored, unimpressed or upset? Then Ira noticed patterns. Aadhya never missed a deadline, quietly fixed errors before anyone asked, and kept a list of everyone's birthdays. One Friday Ira said, "I can never tell what you're thinking. Are you okay with my work?" Aadhya paused and said, "Sorry. It's how I stay steady when things are busy. Your work is careful; I was going to tell you." Ira smiled, though she still couldn't read her face.

qa.q: What did Ira notice about Aadhya's habits?
qa.a: That she never missed a deadline, quietly fixed errors before anyone asked and kept a list of everyone's birthdays.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling in the first weeks?
qa.a: Shut out and unsure, since she read Aadhya's flat face as coldness.

qa.q: What worked for Ira in understanding Aadhya?
qa.a: Noticing patterns over time and then asking directly.

qa.q: What did Aadhya's flat expression mean to her?
qa.a: A way to stay steady when things are busy, and not disinterest. 🙂

grounding: A young adult keeps a blank, even manner in a serious workplace, which can signal composure, disinterest or strain, so meaning came from patterns and asking.

subtype: Deadpan and impassive as professional style [Mismatch]
passage:
Subject: About my meeting face

Dear Naveen,
You asked last week whether I'm unhappy with the team, and I said no but didn't explain, so let me try properly. In meetings I keep my face and voice even. In my last job, showing reactions in front of clients cost us a deal, and I learned to stay blank. That habit followed me here. It doesn't mean I'm bored. It's also fair to say that on Tuesday I was tired after a bad night, and that may have looked like disinterest. If you'd like a sign from me, I can say "good idea" aloud when I think so, and if something is wrong I will say that too. Thanks for asking directly.

Farhan

qa.q: When did Farhan say the tiredness happened?
qa.a: On Tuesday.

qa.q: What was Farhan worried about when building the habit of a blank face?
qa.a: That showing reactions in front of clients might lose them a deal, as it once did.

qa.q: What did Farhan offer to help Naveen read Farhan?
qa.a: To say "good idea" aloud when Farhan thinks so, and to say if something is wrong.

qa.q: How might Naveen have felt before asking?
qa.a: Uncertain whether Farhan was unhappy, which is why Naveen asked directly.

grounding: A young adult explains that their blank, even manner in a serious workplace is composure, though tiredness can look like disinterest, and offers a clearer signal.

subtype: Detached, weary and neutral at work [Interpreting]
passage: Wednesday night. Anirban's notes. Jeevan sat through the whole stand-up with his eyes half-open, answering in single words. My first thought was "lazy," and then "burnt out." Both are labels, and I don't know either. At lunch he ate alone and looked flat. I stopped myself from telling the team he was checked out. Instead I sat down and said, "You seem a bit low on energy this week. No pressure, but how are you finding things?" He said he's been up with his baby daughter every night and is just running on empty. So not lazy. Not even sad, just tired. I offered to take one of his tickets tomorrow and he said he'd think about it. I'm glad I asked before I told anyone anything.

qa.q: Why was Jeevan running on empty?
qa.a: He had been up with his baby daughter every night.

qa.q: What was Anirban thinking while watching Jeevan through the stand-up?
qa.a: First "lazy" and then "burnt out," but Anirban realised they were labels that could not be confirmed.

qa.q: What could Anirban do next?
qa.a: Anirban can follow up on the offer to take a ticket and keep checking in kindly without telling others. 🙂

qa.q: How might Jeevan have felt about being asked?
qa.a: Perhaps relieved to be noticed kindly instead of judged, since he opened up about the sleepless nights.

grounding: A young professional sees a coworker looking flat and tired, and replaces labelling with kind curiosity.

subtype: Detached, weary and neutral at work [Interpreting]
passage:
Nilesh: Hey, you okay? You seemed quiet in the meeting
Tarun: yeah fine
Nilesh: I won't guess what's up. Just checking in, no pressure 🙂
Tarun: honestly just tired. I've been on the night release all week
Nilesh: That would do it. Want me to cover the 4 pm sync?

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling behind the quiet manner?

qa.q: What made Nilesh's check-in kind?

qa.q: How might Tarun have felt if Nilesh had said "You look angry"?

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
subtype: Culture and gender norms about visible reactions [Mismatch]
passage: I'm Rashmi. In my family, tears were for private rooms; my father would say "Be strong" and that was that. When Yash's grandmother passed away, his whole family cried openly at the funeral, hugging and wailing, and I stood stiff at the edge, thinking I ought to be doing something. Yash noticed and whispered, "You don't have to cry, my family just does it that way." I felt hot with embarrassment. Later I said, "In my house we didn't show it. It doesn't mean I felt less." He said, "I thought maybe you didn't care." We both laughed sadly. I still don't cry easily, but I hold his hand now, and he doesn't take it as coldness.

qa.q: What did Yash whisper to Rashmi at the funeral?
qa.a: That Rashmi did not have to cry, and that his family just does it that way.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling at the edge of the funeral?
qa.a: Stiff and embarrassed, and unsure what Rashmi ought to be doing.

qa.q: What helped Rashmi and Yash understand each other?
qa.a: They told each other what showing or hiding tears meant in their own families, and asked instead of assuming.

qa.q: How did Yash first read Rashmi's dry eyes?
qa.a: He thought maybe Rashmi didn't care.

grounding: Families differ on whether crying is encouraged or discouraged, so a young adult and their partner ask what tears and their absence mean to each.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
subtype: Culture and gender norms about visible reactions [Mismatch]
passage: Note from Omkar, project supervisor. After the site accident review, Tushar's eyes filled and he turned away. Two colleagues joked, "Big man crying?" and Tushar went red and left the room. I followed after a few minutes and asked, "Would you like to talk, or just have some space?" He wanted space. Later he told me that where he grew up, crying was seen as weak for men, and his father had always said so. He said his skin flushes easily and people read it as embarrassment, but it can also be anger or heat. I asked how he felt instead of assuming. He said, "Sad, honestly. The colleague who was hurt is a friend of mine." I asked the two colleagues to leave the jokes out, and told Tushar the company counsellor is there if he wants.

qa.q: What did the two colleagues say to Tushar?
qa.a: "Big man crying?"

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling, according to what he told Omkar?
qa.a: Sad, because the colleague who was hurt is a friend of his; his red face could mean embarrassment, anger or heat, so it could not have told Omkar that.

qa.q: What did Omkar do that helped?
qa.a: He offered a choice of talking or space, asked instead of assuming, and asked the colleagues to stop joking.

qa.q: How might Tushar's upbringing shape how he experiences tears?
qa.a: He grew up hearing that crying was weak for men, so he may feel ashamed when tears come.

grounding: Cultural and gender norms shape how tears and blushing are read, so a supervisor asks how a young man feels instead of assuming.
